title: Eighteen Round a Circle
statement:
Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{18}$ be a sequence of $18$ integers, each initially equal to $0$, $1$ or $2$, with indices read modulo $18$, so that $x_{19} = x_1$ and $x_0 = x_{18}$. In one step, every term is replaced simultaneously: for each $i$ with $1 \le i \le 18$, the new value of $x_i$ is $x_{i-1} + x_i + x_{i+1}$, computed from the values before the step, and no reduction is applied to the results.

Let $N$ be the number of the $3^{18}$ possible initial sequences for which, after some number of steps (possibly none), all $18$ terms are multiples of $3$. Here $0$ counts as a multiple of $3$. Find the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$.
hints: Only the residues modulo $3$ matter. Work out what three steps do to a term modulo $3$, by expanding the coefficients of $x_{i-3}, x_{i-2}, \dots, x_{i+3}$. Then ask what the pattern suggests for nine steps.

Let $S$ be the cyclic shift, so one step is the operator $T = S^{-1} + 1 + S$. Use the "freshman's dream": for commuting operators, $(A + B + C)^3 \equiv A^3 + B^3 + C^3 \pmod 3$, because every other multinomial coefficient is $3$ or $6$. Apply this twice to $T$ to find $T^9$, remembering that $S^{18} = 1$.

Modulo $3$, nine steps turn $x$ into the sequence $y$ with $y_i \equiv x_i - x_{i+9}$. This $y$ satisfies $y_{i+9} \equiv -y_i$, so nine more steps send $y$ to $-y$. Hence if $y \not\equiv 0$, the sequence is nonzero after every multiple of nine steps, and all zeros can never be reached. It remains to count the initial sequences with $y \equiv 0$.
solution: Each new term is an integer combination of the old terms, so the residues modulo $3$ after a step depend only on the residues before it. From now on we work modulo $3$. Let $(Sx)_i = x_{i+1}$ be the cyclic shift, so that one step is the linear operator $T = S^{-1} + 1 + S$, and $S^{18} = 1$. For commuting operators $A, B, C$ we have $(A + B + C)^3 \equiv A^3 + B^3 + C^3 \pmod 3$, since all other multinomial coefficients in the expansion are $3$ or $6$. Applying this twice gives $T^3 \equiv S^{-3} + 1 + S^3$ and then $$T^9 \equiv S^{-9} + 1 + S^9.$$ Since $S^{18} = 1$, we have $S^{-9} = S^9$, so $T^9 \equiv 1 + 2S^9 \equiv 1 - S^9$. Therefore nine steps send $x$ to the sequence $y$ given by $y_i \equiv x_i - x_{i+9}$. Suppose first that $x_{i+9} \equiv x_i$ for all $i$. Then $y \equiv 0$, so after nine steps all terms are multiples of $3$. Suppose instead that $y \not\equiv 0$. Then $y_{i+9} \equiv x_{i+9} - x_{i+18} = x_{i+9} - x_i \equiv -y_i$, that is, $S^9 y \equiv -y$. Hence $T^9 y \equiv y - S^9 y \equiv 2y \equiv -y$. By induction, $T^{9m} x \equiv \pm y \not\equiv 0$ for every $m \ge 1$. If some $T^k x$ were zero modulo $3$, then all later stages would also be zero, because $T$ is linear. In particular $T^{9m} x$ would be zero for any $m$ with $9m \ge k$, which is a contradiction. So this sequence never becomes all multiples of $3$. Thus the required condition is exactly $x_{i+9} \equiv x_i \pmod 3$ for all $i$. Since all initial terms lie in $\{0, 1, 2\}$, this means $x_{i+9} = x_i$ for all $i$. Such a sequence is determined by a free choice of $x_1, \dots, x_9$, so $N = 3^9 = 19683$. The remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$ is $683$. Why this works. modular-arithmetic, binomial-theorem, periodicity: cubing modulo $3$ collapses nine steps to a single comparison of terms half a cycle apart, and the $18$-periodicity of the indices makes that comparison decide the outcome exactly.
